<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases—B's captivity/lock-in framing (number portability analogy, "exit with your people") against A's third-party consent and weaponization concerns (Cambridge Analytica, scraper/stalker risk). The debate turned on whether authenticated, scoped graph transfer is workable. B scored real points by showing platforms already display/import relational data for their own growth, forcing A to refine into an "accountability boundary" distinction. But A's sharpest hit—that there is no existing licensing/authentication regime for vetting "legitimate competing platforms" (unlike payment networks' decades of AML law)—was never squarely answered in B's rebuttal 2 or closing; B instead reasserted that the souvenir alternative is toothless without rebutting the enforcement gap. A also used the pressure-question exchange to extract a concrete (if narrow) alternative and closed with the last word, sharpening the "harm-or-moat" dilemma that B's closing did not dismantle. B's cost-flip argument (burden falls on incumbent-exporter, not challenger-recipient) was a genuine strength A only partially rebutted. On balance, A's unanswered enforcement point and stronger final framing give it a modest, competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's rebuttal 2 (A4.3–A4.6), naming a narrow acceptable alternative and arguing the payment-network liability analogy fails absent an equivalent licensing regime for verifying "legitimate competitors"—a point B's subsequent closing did not directly rebut.</best_rebuttal>
